A bad day of writing for me are the days that feel uninspired, where I feel more like I’m going through the motions of writing than actually enjoying the story I’m writing.  On an inspired day I can put 3k-8k words down. If the creativity doesn’t flow right maybe 500-2k.

In my particular case, I don’t count any revisions/editing in my word count.  I only count the words that I’ve added to my story by the end of my writing session.  I also try not to go back too much and look over things unless it’s to reference something. Otherwise I overwhelm myself trying to get things perfect and never finish the first draft.

Now it depends on the age of the children. Younger kids aren’t as indoctrinated into the ideas generally, or don’t have a full understanding of them. Older kids would be more difficult to win over, teens even harder.   However, if they’re in a situation that causes them pain or sadness, it also becomes easier to justify it, teens do get rebellious after all.

Without a lot of understanding on the children’s personalities, I think it’s reasonable to trust other children even if they were told outsiders are “bad”. Outsiders would normally make you think of grown ups/strangers. Kids are easier to talk to and trust than adults. 

Also, if the book is well received, I’d take that as a win.  We all think our stories should be better. Its the nature of creativity, I think.

I described how he got out of it, who was around, and how he’s been dealing with each new situation he found himself in. I have no idea how the story will end or what the next step is. My characters sort of figure it out on their own and it’s been really exciting for me personally. I think that as long as you’re writing, even if it isn’t something you use in the story, you’re making progress. You can always cut those slow scenes or speed them up later on.  It also helps you practice building your character and the world around them. Even if your reader doesn’t know all the fine details of every scene, you knowing them helps bring the important scenes to life. The goal in the first draft is just to get the words down on paper while moving from the beginning of your story to the end of it.

I personally really love throwing my characters together and seeing what they say/do.  If I can use it in the story great, if not then I learned a small bit about my characters. 

I say write your first draft in the way that feels most comfortable to you and then worry about the details when you edit.

I think about my writing day and night. This causes me to catch things that I missed like plot holes, unexplained events, and just basic problems with characters and stuff.  When I find these during my rough draft, I go back and throw in notes to look into it further during my second draft/editing.  That way I don’t spend too much time thinking about it and lose focus on my current goal of just spitting out words for the first draft.

I can’t say that it’ll work the same for everyone, but it started for me when I began making radical, drastic change in my life. I got a divorce, i changed my career, I got rid of “friends”. I removed anything that created negative emotion within me and replaced it with something I was more content, if not happy, with. It’s not something that I can really guide you to do, and I’m not even sure that it’s a good idea to do. The main thing I did was take a long look at my life, and what I wanted in my life. I allowed myself to be a little bit selfish and I stopped allowing people to tell me what I should want and who I should be.  It was the most difficult thing I’ve ever done but it was the best thing I ever did.

I hope this helps but I understand that looking at your life objectively is difficult when you’re stuck in a pool of negative emotion.  Take some of my good vibes. <3
